page: OVHcloud a10-45 is a GPU-accelerated server belonging to the Cloud GPU family. It features 30 dedicated physical cores powered by an AMD EPYC 9554 processor running at 3.3 GHz on the x86_64 architecture under a KVM hypervisor. The hardware configuration includes 42.0 GB of RAM, which provides 1.4 GB per core, and a bundled 400 GB local SSD. Graphics acceleration is delivered by a single NVIDIA A10 GPU from the Ampere family, equipped with 24 GB of VRAM. Network connectivity is rated at a baseline bandwidth of 8 Gbps, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

In benchmark evaluations, the server demonstrates strong performance across multiple compute and memory metrics. Stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU tests place the instance in the top 25%, a tier also matched by its Passmark CPU score and extended instructions performance. Memory bandwidth for small cached blocks is strong, though large block read and write operations fall into the average category. The system excels in database operations and Redis SET operations, both scoring in the top 25%.

The integrated NVIDIA A10 GPU delivers top-tier performance in the top 10% for large language model inference when processing prompts and generating text with small 135M and medium 7B models. Prompt processing for large 70B models remains strong, placing in the top 25%. However, a notable hardware tradeoff is evident in text generation for large 70B models, which falls into the bottom 10% due to the memory capacity constraints of a single 24 GB VRAM GPU.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the server offers a high density of dedicated AMD EPYC compute cores and dedicated GPU acceleration relative to its overall resource profile. The allocation of 30 physical cores with a single thread per core ensures predictable execution without hyperthreading overhead. This configuration is highly suited for small-to-medium LLM inference, software compilation, database operations, and GPU-accelerated rendering tasks, whereas workloads requiring massive memory-to-CPU ratios or large-scale LLM text generation may require alternative configurations.
